description: SpaceHealth es una propuesta de software médico orientada a apoyar el monitoreo y la gestión de la salud de astronautas durante misiones espaciales. El proyecto busca explorar tecnologías.
summary: SpaceHealth Guardian is an autonomous health intelligence and clinical support platform designed to safeguard astronaut well-being during long-duration space missions. Addressing communication latency and the absence of immediate Earth-based clinical support, the platform integrates predictive health monitoring, automated medical triage, and real-time biometric analysis into an intuitive mission dashboard. By combining proactive risk assessment with structured clinical protocols, SpaceHealth Guardian empowers crew members to detect physiological anomalies early, manage medical contingencies independently, and maintain mission resilience in deep space environments where conventional telemedicine is unfeasible.
details:
What the project does

SpaceHealth Guardian is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring prototype built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 “Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions” challenge. Crew members record vital signs, lifestyle data and symptoms. The application compares each measurement with the astronaut’s own 30-day median baseline, separated by rest and exercise context, and runs a deterministic, explainable assessment engine. The result includes a status, the rules that fired, supporting evidence, a plain-language explanation, missing or stale data, related body systems, recommended next steps, references and limitations. A red-flag combination such as chest pain with breathing difficulty immediately instructs the user to contact the crew medical officer and start the applicable emergency procedure, regardless of the Earth link or any AI provider.

The app includes an interactive 2D anatomical digital twin covering ten body systems, a six-environment mission simulator (ISS, lunar transit, lunar base, Mars transit, Mars surface and return to Earth), three judge-ready mission-rescue scenarios, a medical inventory that determines which measurements are realistically possible, a report queue with connected/delayed/disconnected/simulation states, and JSON, CSV and PDF reporting. It also includes a NASA Science module with real ISS radiation data, the five NASA HRP spaceflight hazards, NASA HRP risk and ongoing-research material, and Canadian Space Agency radiation and space-science resources. A built-in retrieval-based assistant explains results and hazards without an API key or internet connection. Optional Ollama, Gemini and OpenAI providers can be configured, but they cannot downgrade an urgent deterministic alert.

How it works and the technology used

The web and desktop applications share one React + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind CSS codebase. React Router provides navigation, Recharts renders trends, Dexie/IndexedDB stores measurements, symptoms, inventory, reports and settings locally, and Lucide supplies icons. The assessment engine and baseline logic are framework-independent TypeScript modules. The web build is an installable PWA using vite-plugin-pwa and Workbox for precaching. The desktop build runs in Electron with context isolation, sandboxing, a minimal contextBridge preload API, validated IPC, CSP and a stable userData directory; electron-builder produces a portable Windows x64 executable. The NASA dosimetry dataset was retrieved from NASA CDAWeb/SPDF (ISS_DOSANL_TEPC, 2015-01-01 to 2015-01-15 UTC; 19,685 raw samples, 333 hourly aggregates), preserving absorbed dose rate (µGy/min) and dose-equivalent rate (µSv/min) as separate quantities. Testing uses Vitest and React Testing Library, plus Puppeteer-based end-to-end smoke tests. Python tooling supports asset generation, NASA data processing and the seven-slide presentation. No server, database, proprietary hardware, cloud account or AI credential is required. The only hardware needed is a standard x64 PC or a modern browser; medical devices are represented by a software inventory, not by connected sensors.

Benefits and intended impact

The project targets the operational gap created by communication delays and blackouts on future lunar and Mars missions. Instead of waiting for Earth, a crew can record data, recognize deterioration, escalate an emergency, and prepare a structured medical report that remains queued locally until the link returns. Personal baselines reduce dependence on generic population thresholds, while the rule trace, evidence and missing-data list make every result reviewable by a crew medical officer. The same design can support remote terrestrial clinics, isolated research stations and telehealth in low-connectivity regions. The intended impact is safer, more autonomous health monitoring and better handovers — not diagnosis or replacement of clinicians. The prototype has not been clinically validated, and any operational use would require review by flight surgeons, regulatory assessment and certified devices.

Creativity

The creative core is the combination of a personalized baseline, an explainable rule engine and a communication-state-aware workflow: the app behaves differently and honestly when the Earth link is delayed or absent. The digital twin is used as a navigation and explanation layer, not as a decorative 3D model. The three rescue scenarios turn a feature tour into a complete clinical-operations story, including an urgent event with no Earth connection and a locally stored report that changes state when the simulated link recovers. The local assistant is explicitly retrieval-based rather than being presented as a trained language model.

Factors considered

The team prioritized medical safety (no diagnosis, no prescriptions, immediate red-flag escalation, persistent disclaimers), privacy (local-only storage, no automatic health-data transmission, no telemetry), auditability (provenance, units, source URLs and limitations), offline resilience, accessibility (text labels in addition to colour), bilingual English/Spanish support, honest labelling of synthetic data, and licensing. The project uses original visual identity, contains no NASA logos, does not imply NASA endorsement, includes only fictional adult astronauts, and documents all NASA and Space Agency Partner sources actually used.

Short version (if the form has a character limit)

SpaceHealth Guardian is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring prototype. Crew members record vitals and symptoms; the app compares them with a personal 30-day median baseline and runs a deterministic, explainable assessment that returns evidence, missing data, next steps and limitations. Chest pain with breathing difficulty triggers immediate crew-medical-officer escalation, independent of the Earth link or AI. It includes an interactive 2D digital twin, six mission environments, three rescue scenarios, a medical inventory, and a local report queue with JSON/CSV/PDF export. The app also integrates real NASA ISS TEPC dosimetry, NASA HRP hazards and risk material, and Canadian Space Agency resources. It is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, IndexedDB and Electron, and ships as a PWA and a portable Windows x64 executable. The built-in assistant is retrieval-based and works without an API key; optional external providers cannot override urgent alerts. The design emphasizes autonomy during communication delays, privacy, explainability, accessibility and honest limitations. It is an experimental educational prototype, not a certified medical device, and has not been clinically validated.
